newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch Rabobank launches limited recourse notes.
newsitem.headline: Dutch Rabobank launches limited recourse notes.

text.p: Dutch co-operative bank Rabobank Nederland on Thursday launched a Limited Recourse Debt Issuance Programme in which investors will assume the transfer and political risks of selected countries.
Rabobank said it would raise up to $250 million by issuing notes with terms of between one month and 30 years.
Bank officials said the first tranche would be between $5 million and $15 million of floating rate five-year notes linked to the country risk of Chile.
It said investors would assume the transfer and political risk of the specific countries in their respective tranches.

"The proceeds of the notes will be used to finance customers of the bank in those selected countries," Rabobank said in a statement. The bank said the programme had been developed over past months with internal and external specialists.
The programme especially enabled it to service customers operating in Latin America and Eastern Europe focusing on food and agribusiness and health care.
If payments under the notes are suspended due to an event in a particular country, the suspension will remain in place until the event ends or two years after the maturity date.
If the second anniversary occurs first, Rabobank would call a meeting of noteholders to propose a solution.
But the notes would continue to accrue interest at the original bond coupon rate during the suspension.
"In this way, Rabobank Nederland has no exposure to the currency risks associated with the nominated country," it said.
Rabobank International is the arranger of the programme.
The other dealers are ABN AMRO, Bear Stearns, Citibank, Daiwa Securities, Goldman Sachs and SBC/Warburg.

"We have more and more customers abroad with offices in emerging markets who want to borrow from us in those currencies," Haijo Dijkstra, head of funding and structures for Rabobank International, told Reuters.
"But as a bank we have a quite stringent policy on country risk and how much exposure we can have in those countries. This is a way of increasing the lines of credit to those countries."
He said he expected the notes, which will be unrated, would sell at a premium to other bonds of Rabobank, which has a AAA credit rating, because investors would carry the country risk.
